Let \(F=\mathbb F_3\), \(K=\mathbb F_{3^6}\), and let \(\chi\) denote the quadratic character of \(K^\times\).

Choose a regular indecomposable pencil \(W=\langle A,B\rangle\) with \(A\) invertible, and put \(T=A^{-1}B\). Since \(B\) is symmetric, \(T\) is self-adjoint for the symmetric bilinear form defined by \(A\). Since \(T\) has irreducible minimal polynomial of degree \(6\), we may identify the underlying vector space with \(K\), with \(T\) acting as multiplication by some degree-\(6\) element \(\alpha\in K\).

Every symmetric bilinear form for which multiplication by \(\alpha\) is self-adjoint has the form

\[
\beta_c(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(cxy),\qquad c\in K^\times.
\]

Multiplying the \(K\)-coordinate by \(u\in K^\times\) replaces \(c\) by \(cu^2\), so for a fixed \(\alpha\) there are exactly two possibilities, according to the square-class of \(c\). Frobenius conjugacy identifies \(\alpha,\alpha^3,\dots,\alpha^{3^5}\), and preserves the square-class.

Now changing the basis of the pencil by

\[
(A,B)\mapsto (aA+bB,\; rA+sB)
\]

replaces

\[
\alpha \mapsto \frac{r+s\alpha}{a+b\alpha},
\qquad
[c]\mapsto [c(a+b\alpha)].
\]

Thus the desired orbits are the orbits of

\[
\Omega=\{(\alpha,\varepsilon): \alpha\in K \text{ has degree }6,\ \varepsilon\in K^\times/K^{\times 2}\}
\]

under \(\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)\times PGL_2(F)\). We count them by Burnside.

There are

\[
3^6-3^3-3^2+3=729-27-9+3=696
\]

degree-\(6\) elements of \(K\), so the identity fixes \(2\cdot 696=1392\) points of \(\Omega\).

Write elements of \(PGL_2(3)\cong S_4\) by their cycle type on \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_3)\):

\[
1,\quad 6\text{ transpositions},\quad 3\text{ double transpositions},\quad 8\text{ elements of order }3,\quad 6\text{ elements of order }4.
\]

Let the Frobenius power be \(\sigma^i:x\mapsto x^{3^i}\), \(i=0,\dots,5\).

For \(i=0\), only the identity Möbius transformation fixes degree-\(6\) elements.

For \(i=1,5\), no degree-\(6\) element can be fixed: the Frobenius orbit would have length dividing the order of the Möbius element, hence at most \(4\), or else the element is fixed by a nontrivial fractional linear map and has degree at most \(2\).

For \(i=2,4\), only order-\(3\) Möbius elements contribute. Take \(m(x)=x+1\). For \(i=2\),

\[
\alpha=\sigma^2(m\alpha)
\iff
\alpha^9=\alpha-1.
\]

This affine equation has \(9\) solutions, a coset of \(\mathbb F_9\). Exactly \(3\) lie in \(\mathbb F_{27}\), and none lie in \(\mathbb F_9\), so exactly \(6\) have degree \(6\). The same count holds for \(i=4\). The denominator is \(1\), so both square-classes are fixed. Contribution:

\[
8\cdot 2\cdot (2\cdot 6)=192.
\]

For \(i=3\), only order-\(2\) Möbius elements contribute.

For a split involution, take \(m(x)=-x\). Then

\[
\alpha=\sigma^3(m\alpha)
\iff
\alpha^{27}=-\alpha.
\]

This is a \(27\)-element trace-zero space over \(\mathbb F_{27}\). Removing \(0\) and the two degree-\(2\) elements satisfying \(x^2=-1\), we get \(24\) degree-\(6\) elements. Again the denominator is \(1\), so both square-classes are fixed. There are \(6\) such involutions, giving

\[
6\cdot (2\cdot 24)=288.
\]

For a nonsplit involution, take \(m(x)=-1/x\). Then

\[
\alpha=\sigma^3(m\alpha)
\iff
\alpha^{27+1}=-1.
\]

There are \(28\) solutions, and \(24\) have degree \(6\), but the denominator is \(\alpha\). Since \(N_{K/\mathbb F_{27}}(\alpha)=-1\), and \(-1\) is nonsquare in \(\mathbb F_{27}\), such \(\alpha\) is nonsquare in \(K\). Hence the square-class flips, so no point of \(\Omega\) is fixed.

Therefore Burnside gives

\[
\frac{1392+192+288}{|\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)|\cdot |PGL_2(3)|}
=
\frac{1872}{6\cdot 24}
=
13.
\]

\[
\boxed{13}
\]
